confirmed.description: The Chaul memory version of Keshavrao is hard to recognise as him. The top frame edge cuts off the top of his head, and the caption 'The dungeon had scraped that away.' covers his chest, sash, sword and most of the horse. What shows of his face is paler and rounder than the present-day Keshavrao in the same panel, with reddened open lips, so the reader cannot easily tell that the rider is the same young man.
confirmed.evidence: Zoomed crop of the right-hand memory area of page-05.png, panel 5.2: the rider's forehead and hair are clipped at the top border, and the caption box fills the middle of the inset from the face down to the saddle. Script 5.2 asks for 'The same young face', with the white angarkha, sash, sheathed sword and bay horse all readable.

verdict.reason:
The identity complaint does not hold, but a small layout fault is real, so this is minor, not major. I zoomed into the right-hand memory inset on page-05.png, panel 5.2.

What is wrong:
- **Head:** the crown of the curly hair touches the top border and is cut by a few pixels. The forehead, brows, eyes and mouth are all inside the frame, so the claim that the forehead is clipped is wrong.
- **Caption:** the box "The dungeon had scraped that away." does sit in the middle of the inset. It covers the rider's chest and upper torso, from just under the chin to the saddle.

What still reads, as script 5.2 asks:
- The face and the mouth open in song.
- Bareheaded, with the hair loose to the shoulders.
- White angarkha cloth below the box, and red sash ends at the left.
- The scabbard tip and fittings of a sword, under the box.
- A bay horse's head, neck and bridle, so the claim that most of the horse is hidden is overstated.
- Palms, a church tower and smoke behind him.

Identity:
- The memory face is narrower, not rounder. A faint moustache shadow matches the ch2 lock in CONTINUITY.md and the 07-keshavrao-v15c sheet.
- It looks paler because the script asks for a warm-toned memory.
- It looks different from the present Keshavrao because the script deliberately gives him uncut hair to the shoulders.
- The red lips are an open, singing mouth. At print size the face is only about a quarter inch tall, so this reads as song.
- The caption "Near Chaul he dared the Portuguese to shoot the song out of his mouth", together with present-day Keshavrao in the same panel, tells the reader who the rider is.

Fix at lettering: move the second caption lower or to one side, and drop the inset art slightly so the hair clears the border. No redraw is needed.

confirmed.description: The chain gang's clothing breaks continuity with 1.5. All five men climbing the stair wear the same clean cream knee-length tunic with a tied sash. The six-man chain in 1.5 wore varied torn grey, brown and off-white rags, and Keshavrao's grey-brown tunic is missing from a line he must be in.
confirmed.evidence: In 2.1 five near-identical cream tunics with sashes climb the stair, collar to collar. In 1.5 the same chain shows Keshavrao in a torn grey-brown tunic, two greybeards in brown rags and Nagoji in ochre.

verdict.reason: Confirmed on close crops. In 2.1, all five climbing prisoners wear the same clean cream knee-length tunic with a tied cloth sash. They look like a uniformed group, not captives in rags. The panel comes straight after 1.5, where the same chain wears varied torn grey, brown and off-white sleeveless rags. The script asks for that variety in 1.1, 1.5, 3.2 and 4.1, and the bible gives Keshavrao and the others prisoner rags. It is the biggest element in a full-width panel, so it is easy to see at print size: the line reads as a different group of men. It is also inconsistent with 2.2, where the same prisoners are back in ragged cloth with bare shoulders. The claim that Keshavrao is missing is weaker. The cast list for 2.1 is empty and Nagoji is not shown either, so this can be read as just part of the chain. That half alone would not count as a defect. The costume break is a real, localized continuity error that needs a redraw of this panel only, so major is the right severity, not blocker.

confirmed.description: The prisoners in the courtyard wear no iron collars and have no collar-to-collar chain. They read as a loose crowd of more than six men with single chains hanging from their wrists, although 1.5, 2.1 and 2.3 lock every man into a collar on one chain.
confirmed.evidence: Zoomed crop of the foreground: the long-haired man raising his arm has a bare neck and one wrist cuff with a long chain hanging from it. The other heads in the front row show no collars and no linking chain.

verdict.reason: I'm confirming this one. I zoomed into panel 2.2 at full resolution (crops of the left half, the right half, the central figure and the right front row). The long-haired man in the centre foreground, raising his right arm, has bare skin at the nape between his hair and his shoulder cloth. He wears no iron collar and no ring, only one wrist cuff with a long chain hanging down. The man at front left has a wrist cuff only. In the right front row, three or four heads show bare or cloth-covered necks and no collars. The one length of chain there lies over a cloth-covered back and is not fixed to any collar. There are about ten prisoners, huddled in a loose crowd, not six men in a collared line. The panel sits between 2.1 (collars on one chain) and 2.3 and 2.5 (Nagoji's collar and chain prominent). Script 1.5 puts every man in a hinged collar on one chain, 2.1 repeats it, and CONTINUITY.md gives Nagoji a collar for chapter 2. So the script's "chained hands" for 2.2 does not allow dropping the collars. The central bare-necked man is the largest figure in a full-width panel, so the gap shows at print size. It is a localized irons error, not wrong identity, lettering or a missing beat, so the severity is major, not blocker. The fix is to redraw the front row with collars on one chain running collar to collar.

confirmed.description: The chain setup and spacing change between 4.3 and 4.4, which is scripted as 'same two-shot'. In 4.3 the two men sit shoulder to shoulder and one slack chain runs from Nagoji's collar to Keshavrao's collar and on to the ring on the right-hand post. In 4.4 they sit well apart and each collar chain rises to the opposite upper corner. A new chain also drops vertically from Nagoji's collar to his wrist manacles.
confirmed.evidence: 4.3: one chain loops Nagoji's collar, then Keshavrao's collar, then the ring on the post at right. 4.4: Nagoji's chain runs up-left out of frame, Keshavrao's runs up-right, a gap of about a body width separates them, and a straight chain runs from Nagoji's collar ring down to his manacles.

verdict.reason: Confirmed on page-04.png, panel 4.4. In 4.3 the two men sit shoulder to shoulder. A single slack chain runs from Nagoji's collar through Keshavrao's collar to the ring on the right-hand post, which is what the script asks for ("one slack chain links both collars to the ring on the beam off to one side"). The script calls 4.4 the "Same two-shot, same sides", but the art changes in three ways. (1) The men sit about a body width apart, with a barrel visible in the gap. (2) The shared chain is gone. Nagoji's chain runs from behind his neck up-left out of the frame, and a separate chain on Keshavrao rises up-right to the top edge. Neither goes to the post ring shown in 4.3. (3) A new straight chain drops from a ring on the front of Nagoji's collar to the chain between his wrist manacles. The CONTINUITY row for chapter 2 gives a collar with the ring at the side and manacles joined by a short chain, and has no collar-to-wrist chain. None of this is too slight to notice. 4.4 is a full-width strip directly under 4.3, and the chains are large and in the foreground. Nothing in the bible or script allows the change. Neither chain hangs taut and vertical above a head, so the forbidden-content rule is not broken. Identity and lettering are fine. This is a localized continuity and costume error, so it is major, not a blocker.

confirmed.description: João's balloon 'Up! Those marked go to the docks.' covers almost all of Nagoji, the foreground figure meant to introduce him. Only his head shows, so the ochre tunic, collar, bandages and ankle irons that identify him in the opening panel cannot be seen. He is also drawn in profile rather than the scripted three-quarter back view.
confirmed.evidence: In the lower right of 1.1, the balloon runs across Nagoji from his chin to the panel edge. Only his curly hair, moustache, ear stud and a bandaged wrist with its manacle peek out below.

verdict.reason: The balloon placement is real, but the reviewer overstates it, so I am downgrading it from major to minor. In 1.1 the balloon "Up! Those marked go to the docks." covers Nagoji's body from just below the chin to the panel's bottom edge, so it does hide most of his costume. Three things argue against major. First, he is still easy to identify. Above the balloon his whole head shows: long loose curls, thick moustache, clean chin and gold ear stud, with the head lifted toward the stair as the script asks. Second, the costume cues are not entirely lost. A strip below the balloon shows the ochre tunic, the bandaged wrist with its iron manacle and chain, and cream cloth, so the claim that the ochre tunic and bandages "cannot be seen" is wrong. Only the ankle irons are fully hidden. Third, the beat still reads. João's call and Nagoji looking up are both clear, the balloon tail points correctly at João, and panel 1.3 shows Nagoji's full captivity costume two panels later. The pose complaint is slight: his body is turned away and only his face is in profile as he looks up and left at the stair. That is close to the scripted three-quarter back view with the head lifted, not wrong. What remains is a lettering polish fix: shrink the balloon or move it left over the stair and wall so it no longer covers the foreground figure. No redraw is needed.

confirmed.description: The balloons read out of order, so the exchange is inverted. Nagoji's reply "It is what I know." sits between his first balloon and Keshavrao's "The sahib still counts chances.", lower than both but overlapping them vertically, with its tail rising to Nagoji's chin. Reading left to right gives: We are not there yet... / It is what I know. / The sahib still counts chances. The reply comes before the line it answers, and that line is a planted beat (adaptation notes).
confirmed.evidence: page-05.png orig px: "We are not there yet" balloon about x400-663, y943-1262; "It is what I know." about x721-996, y1137-1248; "The sahib still counts chances." about x1193-1453, y999-1220. The middle balloon overlaps the right balloon vertically (y1137-1220) and sits to its left, so a left-to-right reader hits it second.

verdict.reason: Confirmed on page 5, panel 3, but I rate it major, not blocker. In the full-resolution crop (orig x360-1480, y935-1285), Nagoji's reply "It is what I know." spans about y1135-1245 and sits right against the lower half of his first balloon. Keshavrao's "The sahib still counts chances." is at the far right, about y1000-1220. The two balloons overlap vertically by about 85 px, and the reply is to the left of the line it answers. So the reply sits in the same horizontal band, between the two balloons it should follow. A reader who finishes "is a chance." near y1180 moves right and reaches "It is what I know." before Keshavrao's line. The same thing happens in a reduction to about 35% scale (roughly print size), where the reply looks like a second Nagoji balloon chained to the first. Keshavrao's balloon starts about 135 px higher, which gives a reader who goes by top edges a weak cue, but it does not outweigh the side-by-side placement. The script (5.3) and adaptation note 233 set the order: Nagoji's first line, Keshavrao's line, Nagoji's "It is what I know.", and days pass only after that line. The render therefore inverts the scripted exchange. It is not a blocker because the text and both tails are correct and the beat is not lost: "The sahib still counts chances." is still clearly Keshavrao's and still follows Nagoji's talk of chance, so the plant survives. The fix is localized to the lettering and needs no art redraw: move "It is what I know." below or to the right of Keshavrao's balloon, for example lower right with its tail running back to Nagoji, or raise Keshavrao's balloon toward the centre above it.

confirmed.description: The caption "The dungeon had scraped that away." covers the Chaul memory inset, which is the visual point of the panel. It hides the young Keshavrao's torso, sash, sword hilt and most of the horse. Only his singing head and the horse's head show above and below the box. The orphan word "away." also wastes a line in the box.
confirmed.evidence: page-05.png orig px: caption box about x1050-1440, y724-853, sitting on the warm-toned memory area (about x1000-1466). Rider's head shows above it at about y660-720; the horse's legs and head show below it.

verdict.reason: Confirmed on page 5, panel 2 after cropping and zooming. The "The dungeon had scraped that away." box sits across the middle of the Chaul memory inset, at about x1050-1440, y724-853 of an inset that spans about x1000-1466, y660-930. That box covers roughly 40% of the inset, right across the rider. The young Keshavrao's chest, upper angarkha, sash knot and sword hilt are hidden. Only his singing head and loose hair show above the box. Below it you see his hand, the white skirt with some loose red sash ends, the tip of the scabbard, and the bay horse's head, neck and tack. The reviewer slightly overstates it: the sash ends, the scabbard tip and the horse's head and neck are still visible. But the main point holds. The inset is the whole reason for the panel, and the script asks for specific memory-costume details (angarkha with sash, sword at the hip). The box cuts the figure into a floating head over a horse and hides the hilt and sash. The beat still reads as a singing rider with musket smoke, so this is not a blocker. It is a clear, localized lettering placement error, so major. The panel has very little free space: the first caption already fills the dark area of the hold, and the sky strip right of the head is only about 230 px wide. So the fix probably needs both captions repositioned or the inset re-cropped, not a small nudge. The orphan word "away." on its own line is minor polish. Rewrapped as two balanced lines, the box would be narrower.

confirmed.description: Keshavrao's off-panel question "Do you know where they send us?" has no tail. The script says it comes from off-panel below. The panel holds no figures, so nothing on the page says who is speaking. The balloon is also jammed against the right panel border and nearly touches the bottom border.
confirmed.evidence: page-04.png orig px: tailless capsule balloon about x1218-1682, y2406-2524; panel right border at x1688. No tail runs toward the bottom edge (checked at full resolution).

verdict.reason: I confirmed the problem at full resolution. On page 4, panel 5, the balloon "Do you know where they send us?" spans about x1218-1682, y2406-2531. Its only tail is a collapsed sliver at the bottom-left corner, about x1234-1236, y2528-2532: a white gap 2 px wide and about 5 px tall. It points sideways and stops at the balloon's own bottom outline, so at 300 DPI it is under 0.2 mm and invisible. The script says this panel has no figures and "The balloon comes from off-panel below" (KESHAVRAO, off, below), and the cast override for page-04-panel-05 is empty. With no figure on screen, the tail is the only thing that can show where the voice comes from, and it does not appear on the page. The crowding is also real. The balloon's right edge is about 6 px (0.5 mm) inside the panel border at x1688. Its bottom outline (y2529-2531) is about 8 px (under 1 mm) above the panel's bottom border (y2539-2541). So there is no room for a downward tail, which is probably why it collapsed. I am not calling it a blocker, because the speaker can still be worked out: Keshavrao speaks in 4.4 just before, "us" means a fellow prisoner, and Nagoji answers "South. That much is certain." at the start of page 5. The fix is limited to the lettering. Move the balloon up and in from the right and bottom borders, then draw a clear tail running off the bottom border, as the script asks. That makes it a major issue (wrong or missing speaker tail, cramped placement), not a blocker.

confirmed.description: Lettering hides the Chaul memory inset. 'The dungeon had scraped that away.' is laid straight across the rider and covers his torso, the white angarkha, the sash, the sword at his hip and most of the bay horse. Only the singing face and part of the horse's head show. 'Near Chaul...' also overlaps the inset's left edge. The image that sets young Keshavrao against the broken boy is mostly lost.
confirmed.evidence: In the second strip, right half (inset about x 750-1057), the caption box spans about x 757-1040, y 523-615 and covers everything between the rider's chin and the horse's bridle. The sword hilt shows only as a sliver below the box.

verdict.reason: Confirmed on page 5, panel 5.2. I checked a zoomed crop of the render (inset at about x 1040-1470, y 660-935 at 1838 px width) against the source frame page-05-panel-02-v11.png. The source frame shows everything the script asks for in the Chaul memory: the white angarkha, the red sash, the sheathed sword hilt at the hip, and the bay horse's head, eye, ears and bridle. In the render, the caption "The dungeon had scraped that away." covers the band from just under the rider's chin to the horse's cheek. That hides the angarkha's chest, the whole sash apart from a few red flecks, most of the sword (only the gold scabbard tip shows below the box), and the horse's ears and eye. What still shows: the long-haired singing face, the smoke and the town above, and the white skirt, one hand and the horse's lower muzzle and bridle below. The SELECTION-MANIFEST-r2 note said the inset sky and the dark hold between the figures were clear for captions, but the reserve actually used for caption 2 (rect 1344-2119 x 251-511 in frame pixels) sits straight on the rider's torso. So this is a lettering-placement error, not something the script or bible allows. The "Near Chaul..." box also cuts into the inset's left edge, which is a smaller issue. The beat is not lost: a young long-haired man singing on horseback before smoke can still be read. That makes it major, not blocker. The fix is to move caption 2 into the dark hold area or the upper sky, or to stack both captions on the left, so the sash, sword and horse show.

confirmed.description: The caption order is likely to invert, and the meaning breaks. The first caption, 'Their eyes told a different story.', is boxed in the top-right corner over the Goan Catholics. The second, 'They weighed the value of the bodies in chains.', sits on the left beside the Hindu merchants. A left-first reader gets 'They weighed...' before its setup. The 'eyes' caption also lands beside the Catholics when it refers to the blank-faced merchants.
confirmed.evidence: In the top strip, 'Their eyes told a different story.' sits at about x 770-1060, y 262-322. 'They weighed the value...' sits at about x 345-760, y 332-395, directly beside the two turbaned merchants in the left doorways.

verdict.reason: I confirmed the problem on page 3, panel 3.1, at 300 DPI. "Their eyes told a different story." sits at about x 1068-1475, y 360-450, touching the top border on the right, over the Goan Catholics. "They weighed the value of the bodies in chains." sits at about x 478-1055, y 460-552, on the left beside the turbaned merchants. The boxes almost touch at the corners and step down from upper right to lower left. That is the standard backward stagger in comic lettering: the left box is big and close to where the eye enters the panel, so many readers will read "They weighed..." first. Neither the script nor CONTINUITY.md sets a placement rule that allows this. The script orders "Their eyes" first. Read in the wrong order, the pair can suggest the merchants' eyes showed something other than calculation, which turns the beat around. There is also a placement problem even in the right order. Page 2 ends on Duarte, and the script gives no spoken setup for the merchants' blank faces, so "Their" must take its meaning from the art. Placed over the Catholics with their hands over their noses, it points the reader at the wrong group. This is a localized, composited lettering fix, not a redraw: move "Their eyes..." to the upper left near the merchants and "They weighed..." below or to the right of it. Major is the right severity.

confirmed.description: The chapter's opening caption order is at risk. 'They woke us under cover of bells.' is boxed in the top-right corner, while 'I counted the strokes.' sits further left in the same band. A left-first read gives 'I counted the strokes' before any bells are mentioned. João's balloon also covers most of Nagoji, so the establishing panel shows only his face and hair, not the ochre tunic, bandaged hands or ankle irons. He is drawn in three-quarter front profile, not the scripted three-quarter back view.
confirmed.evidence: In the top strip, 'They woke us...' sits at about x 855-1172, y 262-325, and 'I counted the strokes.' at about x 410-625, y 327-387. The 'Up! Those marked go to the docks.' balloon (about x 735-1075, y 410-500) sits over Nagoji's body at the right.

verdict.reason: Mostly refuted. One small real issue is left, and it is polish rather than major. (1) Caption order: the two boxes do not share any vertical space. At full resolution, "They woke us under cover of bells." runs from about y 360 to 450 and is pinned to the top-right corner of the panel. The top of "I counted the strokes." is at about y 453, which puts it fully below the first box and roughly a quarter of the panel's height lower. Readers take the box that sits clearly higher first, so the order runs bells, then strokes, then João's balloon in a normal Z path. Even read in reverse, the two lines still make sense. Refuted. (2) "Three-quarter front profile" is wrong. The face is a side profile turned up-left toward João, with the ear, gold stud and the mass of hair at the back of the head facing the viewer. In the unlettered frame (frames/page-01-panel-01-v03.png) his back and shoulder are toward the reader, which is the scripted three-quarter back view with his head lifted. Refuted. (3) Costume coverage: ankle irons, bare feet and most of the dhoti are drawn in the frame, but the layout's visible_rect (0-536 of 759 px) crops them out on purpose. That is a framing choice, not a missing beat. The real issue is that the "Up! Those marked go to the docks." balloon (about x 1020-1495, y 575-695 on the page) sits over Nagoji's collar, shoulder and most of his ochre tunic. Below it, only a bandaged forearm with an iron cuff and chain, a sliver of ochre and the edge of the dhoti show. His identity is still clear (face, moustache, curly hair, gold ear stud), the action of his head lifted toward João still reads, and panels 1.3 and 1.4 on the same page show his full captivity costume. A balloon over the protagonist's torso in the establishing panel is worth nudging left or up toward the stair, but it is minor polish, not a major error.

refuted.description: The Chaul memory inset does not read as Keshavrao, and the caption hides his memory costume. The rider has a full curly mane, no faint moustache and reddened lips, so he looks more like a young Nagoji than 'the same young face'. The caption 'The dungeon had scraped that away.' covers his torso and hip, where the white angarkha, the sash and the sheathed sword should be visible.
refuted.reason:
I zoomed the 5.2 inset at native 300 DPI pixels. It does not support a major finding.

1. **Long hair.** The curly shoulder-length hair is what the script asks for: "his hair uncut and loose to the shoulders, bareheaded". It is not a deviation from Keshavrao.

2. **Not a young Nagoji.** Nagoji's defining marks in the bible are a thick moustache and a clean chin. The inset face has no moustache at all, so it does not read as Nagoji.

3. **Face too small to matter.** The face is about 40 to 60 px tall at 300 DPI, roughly 0.15 to 0.2 in printed. At that size the sheet's faint moustache would be a few pixels and not legible either way. The red mouth reads as an open singing mouth, which is the scripted "mouth open in song". The faint dark dot in the ear is equally invisible at print size.

4. **Identity is clear in context.** The caption says "he". The present-day Keshavrao (short hair, faint moustache, grey-brown tunic) sits in the left half of the same panel, and 5.1 just established him. Readers will take it as his memory.

5. **Costume still reads around the caption.** The caption "The dungeon had scraped that away." does cover the chest to the hip. Even so, the white angarkha shows at the collar and in the white skirts flaring below the box. A red sash shows below the caption. The sheathed sword with its brass chape hangs by the horse's shoulder, and the bay horse and musket smoke are clear. Every scripted element of the memory still reads, so this is lettering polish, not a localized costume error.

Optional fixes: move that caption up over the sky and church area so more of the torso and sash shows, and tone down the lip red on a regen. Neither needs a redraw.

refuted.description: The officer is meant to be seen only in silhouette. Instead he is drawn in a lit dark navy-blue coat with gold buttons, a gold-trimmed tricorne, a lace jabot and a red cloak. That reads as a British or Dutch naval blue-coat, which the bible forbids for the Portuguese.
refuted.reason: The art does not show the problem as reported. I zoomed into page 5, panel 5.5 (page-05.png, around x 1080-1470, y 1790-2160 at full resolution). The officer's coat is not navy. I sampled about 37,000 dark coat pixels, and their mean is RGB (37, 27, 25), a warm near-black. Not one of those pixels has blue more than 8 above red. Smaller samples of the front, the sleeve and the lower coat all come out neutral too, around (26-37, 23-35, 23-36). The hat is the same near-black. At print size the figure reads as a dark, black-coated European officer in a black tricorne, not a Dutch VOC or British naval blue-coat. The bible's rule (CONTINUITY.md line 128) bars Portuguese figures from reading as British redcoats or Dutch blue-coats. A black coat is neither, and a red cloak over one shoulder is not a red coat. The script asks that he be "seen only in silhouette". The render keeps him strongly backlit with his face fully shadowed, so no identity problem arises. Rim light does pick out small gold buttons, gold edging on the hat brim, a white jabot and cuff, and the red cloak. That is a slight loosening of the silhouette note, not a costume error. The beat still reads (laughing sailors above, a shadowed officer in a tricorne, light falling on the faces in the hold), so at most this is optional polish, not a major problem.

refuted.description: There is an escort soldier walking with the chain gang who reads as a Dutch VOC blue-coat, which breaks the standing rule for Portuguese guards. He wears a blue uniform coat with brass buttons, a leather cross-belt and a black tricorne, and carries a shouldered musket. Every other Portuguese guard in the chapter wears a morion or a broad hat with a buff jerkin. Repaint him in a buff leather jerkin and a morion or broad black hat. Note that a bystander nearby also wears a blue coat, but he is a civilian, which the script allows.
refuted.reason: I'm refuting this because it's too slight to matter at print size. The figure is real. In page-03.png he sits at about x 955-1000, y 595-722 at 300 DPI. Zoomed in 4x, he wears a blue coat with brass buttons, a cross-belt and a black tricorne, with a musket barrel standing above his shoulder. But he is only about 125 px tall, which is about 1 cm in print. His lower body is cut off by the panel border and he is half hidden behind the lead prisoner's back. At native resolution he looks like one more of the three blue-coated, tricorned men in this panel. The other two are the scripted Goan townsmen 'in European-cut coats and breeches' standing just to the right, holding cloths to their faces. At print size the musket is a hairline and the cross-belt can't be made out, so he doesn't clearly read as a guard at all, let alone as a Dutch VOC soldier. Panel 3.1 calls for no guards in the script. The bible rule (CONTINUITY.md line 128) is about Portuguese guards reading as Dutch blue-coats, and this tiny background figure doesn't make that reading at print size. If the author wants extra polish, a later pass could repaint his coat buff or brown. That would be minor at most, not a major.

refuted.description: Keshavrao's two balloons are in the wrong order. "We will sweat for their salvation." sits to the left of "They need men to cut cane..." and overlaps it vertically, so it reads first and his conclusion comes before his premise. His two balloons are also unlinked, and the lower one sits near Nagoji's balloon.
refuted.reason: I zoomed into page 5, panel 1 (crop of orig px x140-1700, y350-660), and the art does not support the claim that the balloons read out of order. "They need men to cut cane..." begins at the same top line as Nagoji's "South. That much is certain." (both about y360 orig). Its first text line, "They need men to cut", sits level with "South. That much is certain.", so after Nagoji's line the eye carries straight right into Keshavrao's premise. All of that balloon's text is above the text of "We will sweat for their salvation." (about y540 orig, top edge about y485, roughly 125 px lower). The layout is therefore a normal Z-path: top-left (Nagoji), top-right (Keshavrao's premise), then lower middle (Keshavrao's conclusion). That matches the script order NAGOJI, KESHAVRAO "They need men", KESHAVRAO "We will sweat". The vertical overlap the reviewer measured exists only because the right balloon is tall. Its top tier is clearly higher, so the lower balloon does not read first. The other points don't hold up either. The script gives two separate KESHAVRAO entries, so two unlinked balloons are allowed. The lower balloon does sit under Nagoji's, but its tail clearly points right to Keshavrao's head, so the speaker is not in doubt. A connector between the two Keshavrao balloons would be optional polish, not a real fault, and the stacking is not ambiguous enough to matter at print size.

refuted.description: Keshavrao's introduction and the absent-hilt plant are both lost. The man two ahead of Nagoji (young, short hair, grey-brown tunic, just right of the guard) is drawn in front three-quarter view, not from behind. His head faces forward-left, not turned toward the whisper. Both manacled hands are held together in front of his groin, so the right hand is not at his hip curled around an absent grip. The adaptation notes say Chapter 3 depends on that grip. The caption 'Keshavrao. One of my riders.' also sits over the two leftmost prisoners, which invites the reader to tag the wrong man.
refuted.reason: I'm refuting this as a major. I zoomed into page 1, panel 1.5 at 3x, and the art does not lose either beat. Keshavrao is exactly where the script puts him, two men ahead of Nagoji. He matches his lock: young, black hair hacked short, faint moustache, softer face, grey-brown torn tunic, no ear stud, no scar. He is also the only figure who looks like that, so he is easy to pick out. The reviewer's main evidence is wrong. His hands are not held together in front of his groin. His right hand (on the viewer's left, since he faces us) is a closed fist at his right hip, at waist height. His left hand reaches across lower down with the chain trailing between them. That is close to the scripted 'right hand hangs at his hip, fingers curled around an absent grip… the left hand trailing with it', and it reads as a clenched hip grip at print size. The same plant appears again at 6.2 anyway. His head is in profile toward the front of the line, away from Nagoji. That still carries 'eyes kept forward' and the page logline, 'a friend who will not look back'. The script also asks for his head turned 'a few degrees toward the whisper', which is too subtle to call a missing beat. What is left is polish. He is shown from the front rather than from behind. His head is not turned slightly back. The guard stands on his left side instead of in the gap between him and Nagoji. The 'Keshavrao. One of my riders.' caption sits in the usual upper-left spot, over the two leftmost men. Captions have no tails, and the distinct young face makes him the obvious match, so a reader will not mistake him for someone else. That is minor at most, not a redraw-level fidelity error.

refuted.description: Duarte's sign of the cross, the must-keep plant for chapters 24 and 25, does not read as a blessing. His index and middle fingers point sideways across his chest beside his pendant cross, so he looks like he is fingering his cassock or his own cross. His eyes are lowered to his chest, not on the chain, and the tightened jaw and involuntary quality are not visible.
refuted.reason: I zoomed into page 2, panel 2.4. The art matches the script's own staging. Script 2.4 is "Tight on Duarte" and says his ink-stained right hand is "raised at his chest, partway through a small, slow sign of the cross." The render shows exactly that: the ink-stained right hand is at his breastbone with the index and middle fingers extended together, which is the Latin two-finger blessing hand. The fingertips rest on the button line at the centre of his chest, above and to the left of the pendant, not on it. That is the sternum point of a sign of the cross frozen partway through, not a hand holding the cross or the cassock. Because the shot is tight, the chain is out of frame, so the script itself rules out a visible gesture toward the prisoners. The face also carries the beat: brows knit, mouth turned down and set, eyes lowered. That reads as regret and something he did not mean to show, and the previous panel (2.3) already showed him meeting Nagoji's eyes. The caption in the same panel, "A blessing, perhaps. Or an apology.", ties the gesture to its meaning, and the narrator's "perhaps" deliberately leaves it ambiguous. A clearer motion cue, such as fingers angled upward or a faint arc of movement, would be optional polish. The beat is present and identifiable at print size, so this is not a major defect.

refuted.description: The exchange is likely to read in the wrong order. Nagoji's reply 'It is what I know.' sits right beside his first balloon and below and left of Keshavrao's 'The sahib still counts chances.' Proximity pulls the eye Nagoji, Nagoji, Keshavrao, so the scene closes on Keshavrao's jab and Nagoji's answer goes unanswered to nothing. The script has Nagoji answering last.
refuted.reason:
I cropped page 5, panel 5.3 at native resolution and the placement follows the normal zig-zag order, so I am refuting this. In the 1120x360 crop, the balloon positions are:
- "We are not there yet..." (Nagoji, left) spans y 15-335.
- "The sahib still counts chances." (Keshavrao, right) has its top at about y 65, and its text runs from about y 125 to 225.
- "It is what I know." (Nagoji) has its top at about y 205, and its text sits at about y 255.

All of Nagoji's reply text is below all of Keshavrao's text. Its top is also lower than the middle of Keshavrao's balloon. That is about 0.47 in of drop in print, on a panel only about 1.1 in tall. Under the usual rule that the higher balloon is read first, the order comes out Nagoji, Keshavrao, Nagoji, which matches the script: left top, then right upper, then back left and lower.

Panel 5.1 on the same page uses the same layout: top-left, then top-right, then lower middle. That shows the letterer applied the higher-first rule consistently.

Nagoji's reply does sit next to the bottom of his first balloon, and its tail clearly goes to Nagoji's chin, so a few readers might read his two balloons in a row. But Keshavrao's balloon sits clearly higher, and the reply is clearly lower. At this print size that is ordinary dialogue placement, not a mistake that needs a redraw. If anything, moving "It is what I know." a little lower or further left would be optional polish.

minors.description: Nagoji's gold ear stud is missing. His visible ear lobe shows an empty piercing hole and no stud. The bible lists the small gold ear stud as part of his constant identity.
minors.evidence: 4x crop of Nagoji's ear at the lower edge of panel 5.5 (page-05.png, about x=480-560, y=1680-1750 at display scale): the lobe has a dark pierced dimple and no gold. His stud is present in 4.4, 5.1, 5.3, 6.1, 6.3 and 6.5.

minors.description: Duarte's hat changes between consecutive panels. In 2.3 it is a battered grey-brown felt hat. In 2.4 and 2.5 it is a crisp black broad-brimmed hat. He should wear the same travel hat throughout the gate sequence.
minors.evidence: page-02.png: the 2.3 crop shows a weathered, mottled brown-grey hat. Panel 2.4 (tight on Duarte) and the back view in 2.5 show a clean black hat with a dark band.

minors.description: The sleeper João cuffs could be mistaken for Nagoji. He is the most prominent prisoner in the panel and has shoulder-length curly black hair, like Nagoji. With a full beard on top of that, readers who just saw Nagoji's long curly hair in 1.1 may briefly read him as a bearded Nagoji. Only his grey rags (not ochre) set him apart.
minors.evidence: Zoom of the right side of panel 1.2 (page-01.png): the prisoner under João's hand has loose curly shoulder-length hair and a thick full beard. A second long-curly-haired, bearded prisoner is cut off at the right edge.

minors.description: Keshavrao's build in 4.4 drifts from his lock. The script asks for 'narrow shoulders' and a slighter frame than Nagoji's, but his shoulders and arms here are as broad and muscular as Nagoji's beside him. That weakens the young/old contrast the two-shots rely on. The same heavy deltoids show again in 6.2.
minors.evidence: Panel 4.4 crop (page-04.png): Keshavrao, hunched over his fists at right, has heavy rounded shoulders and thick upper arms about as wide as Nagoji's at left. In 6.2 (page-06.png) his bare shoulder and arm are similarly muscular.

minors.description: Duarte's hat changes colour within the page. In 2.3 it is a battered grey-brown felt. In 2.2, 2.4 and 2.5 it is a crisp black broad-brimmed hat.
minors.evidence: In 2.3 the brim is mottled grey-brown and worn. In 2.4 the close-up shows a clean flat black hat with a black band. In 2.5 a black hat hangs on his back.

minors.description: Duarte's satchel strap is not consistent. In 2.3 the strap crosses his left shoulder and the bag hangs at his left hip. 2.4, a tight shot, shows no strap at all. In 2.5, seen from behind, the bag hangs at his right hip.
minors.evidence: In 2.3 the brown strap runs over the screen-right shoulder (his left) to the bag at lower right. In 2.4 both shoulders of the cassock are bare of any strap. In 2.5 the bag sits on the screen-right side of his back view, which is his right.

minors.description: The gaol guards' costume varies on page 1. The crouching guard in 1.3 and the guards on the stair in 1.1 wear dark brown quilted leather waistcoats, cream shirts, dark breeches and white stockings, almost identical to João's outfit. The 1.5 guard wears the scripted buff leather jerkin. The script calls for buff jerkins throughout.
minors.evidence: 1.3 guard: morion over a brown waistcoat matching João's, cream shirt, white stockings, buckled shoes. 1.5 guard: morion over a yellow-tan buff jerkin with crossed belts.

minors.description: Nagoji's collar ring moves around. The bible puts it at the side. In 1.3, 1.4, 4.4, 6.1 and 6.5 a ring hangs at the front of the throat, sometimes with a chain dropping to the wrists. In 1.5, 2.5, 3.4 and 4.3 the chain leaves from the side.
minors.evidence: In the 1.3 zoom a ring and links hang centred under his chin. In the 6.5 zoom the front ring carries a chain down to his manacles. In 2.5 the chain exits the side of the collar.

minors.description: The guard stands inside the coffle line, between the third prisoner and Keshavrao, with the collar chain running behind his shoulders. That makes him read as a link in the chain rather than a guard walking alongside it.
minors.evidence: In 1.5 the chain from the grey-bearded third man's collar passes behind the morion-helmeted guard at shoulder height and on to Keshavrao's collar.

minors.description: The prisoners boarding behind the clerk wear red, blue and a yellow-ochre tunic, and show no collars or linking chain. That weakens Nagoji's ochre as 'the one warm note among grey and brown rags' and breaks the collar-chain continuity. The clerk, meant to be a lay clerk, also wears a basket-hilted sword that makes him read as an officer.
minors.evidence: Zoomed crop of the gangway queue: one tunic each in red, blue and yellow, single wrist cuffs, bare necks. The clerk in the brown coat and grey hat has a gilt basket hilt at his left hip.

minors.description: The foreground chain runs from one prisoner's wrist cuff to the next man's wrist, a wrist-to-wrist coffle. Every other panel uses the collar-to-collar chain.
minors.evidence: In 3.1 the chain loops from the left foreground prisoner's manacled wrist across to the wrist of the rag-clad man in the centre.

minors.description: The Portuguese guards on the wharf and deck wear red sashes, and in 3.2 also a red neck and shoulder piece. The script asks for gaol guards with nothing red.

minors.description: A lit lantern hangs right behind the pair in 4.3, immediately after 4.1 shows the guard carrying the only lantern up the ladder as the dark closes in. 5.1 and 5.3 also show several lit lanterns in the hold.
minors.evidence: There is a glowing hanging lantern at the top left of 4.3, behind Nagoji's head.

minors.description: Nagoji's bandages grow longer across the chapter. Pages 1 to 3 match the captivity sheet's short wrist wraps. In 4.3, 4.4 and 6.4 the wraps run from wrist almost to elbow.
minors.evidence: 1.3 zoom: wraps cover about a hand's width above the manacles. 4.4: both forearms are wrapped nearly to the elbow. 6.4: long wraps run the whole visible forearm.

minors.description: The hand gesture is reversed. Nagoji's bandaged hand should reach in from the left and rest on Keshavrao's forearm, with Keshavrao's thin fingers closing over it. Instead Keshavrao's bare hand grips Nagoji's bandaged forearm, and Nagoji's own hand hangs limp below. 6.5 carries the same reversal.
minors.evidence: 6.4: an unbandaged hand coming from the right clasps the long bandaged forearm just above its manacle, and Nagoji's fingers point down beneath it.

minors.description: The props that should carry the first cant do not show it. The dipper hangs plumb on its peg and the water in the trough is level, so 6.1 does not set up the steeper 10-degree tilt of 6.5.

minors.description: The sailor's balloon 'Wind is with us...' covers Nagoji's torso, manacles and hobbled ankles in the middle distance, leaving only his head, so the scripted irons cannot be seen on him.

minors.description: The shipping clerk's hat has a modern shape. It has a pinched, dented crown with a band and a rolled brim, which reads as a 19th or 20th-century fedora or cowboy hat. Worn with his long duster-like coat, it gives him a Western or adventurer look that is out of period for 1738-1753. A low round crown with a flat broad brim, or a tricorne, would fit the period.
minors.evidence: page-03.png, the clerk on the wharf to the right of centre, seen from behind. In the original the hat sits at about x 1095-1320, y 1050-1150. On zoom the crown is clearly creased front to back with a pinch at the front.

minors.description: The chapter's opening captions step from right to left. The first caption, "They woke us under cover of bells.", sits hard in the top-right corner. The second, "I counted the strokes.", sits to its left and lower, where the eye enters a wide strip first. João's balloon also covers foreground Nagoji from the chin down. The script makes Nagoji the foreground figure, and here he is mostly hidden.

minors.description: The same right-to-left caption staircase as 1.1. "Their eyes told a different story." (first) sits top right and "They weighed the value..." (second) sits left and lower.
